summary.text:
Argyll and Bute's mid-year 2025-26 is a full tabular treasury report — not a narrative note — and the reconciliation is unusually clean because the paper prints the arithmetic that ties an outside reader to it. Table 5.4.6 (p11) has PWLB debt at 30 September 2025 of £143.357m at an average 4.50%, alongside a single £5.255m LOBO at 4.75% and £0.356m of temporary loans (total loan debt £148.968m at 4.50%). Our own PWLB file holds 21 loans totalling £142,516,662 at a weighted 4.4746%. The £840k gap is essentially the £0.840m second EIP principal payment that paragraph 5.4.1 schedules for the second half of the year; add it back and our current holding matches the paper's implied year-end 2025-26 PWLB position to about £338. That is the report's own arithmetic doing the reconciliation.

Two things are worth writing about. First, that reconciliation itself: the paper prints its EIP repayment schedule alongside the mid-year external debt total, which is exactly what lets an outside reader footnote it end-to-end. Second, paragraph 5.4.3 records a new £20m PWLB loan at 4.69% maturing 07/04/2028, taken "on a relatively short-term basis" because long-term rates are "relatively high but forecast to steadily fall". MUFG's own forecast in the next section has 5-year PWLB coming off from 4.80% (Sept 2025) to 4.30-4.40% through 2026-27 and 4.20% in 2027-28. The bet becomes falsifiable when the loan matures in April 2028 and needs replacing.

On the balance sheet the identity closes. The revised year-end forecast at 5.3.7 gives CFR £396m, Borrowing £187m, OLTL £102m and prints "Under Borrowing 107" — and paragraph 5.3.8 confirms explicitly that this is the internal borrowing figure. £107m — 27% of the £396m CFR — is funded from internal reserves rather than external debt, which the report describes as a "prudent and cost-effective" but "not risk free" position that will require ongoing review.

One thing we cannot tell. Paragraph 5.4.2 flagged 22 December 2025 as a possible LOBO call date. That date has now passed but the paper closes at 30 September (signed 21 November) so it cannot record the outcome, and we do not hold a separate LOBO-call log for this council. The "Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream" step-up from 4.9% to 7.4% (5.2.3) looks alarming on the page but is IFRS 16 reclassification, not new strain — paragraph 5.2.2 says so.

officer.body:
Hi Carolyn,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, your own PWLB book laid against ours, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. Below are a couple of thoughts on your 2025-26 mid-year review, which Audit and Scrutiny recommended in December and Council received on 29 January. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report prints its EIP repayment schedule alongside the mid-year external debt total, which is exactly what lets a reader outside the council reconcile it end-to-end.

The tie first, because it settles whether we've actually read the paper. Your Table 5.4.6 shows PWLB debt of £143.357m at 30 September at an average 4.50%. We hold 21 PWLB loans totalling £142,516,662 at a weighted 4.4746%. The difference is £840,338 — essentially the £0.840m second EIP principal payment that paragraph 5.4.1 schedules for the second half of the year. Add that back and our file matches your paper's implied year-end position to about £338. The two-and-a-half basis points on the average rate is the routine gap between effective-interest accounting and the nominal rate.

The £20m PWLB loan at 4.69% maturing 07/04/2028 is your paper's own dated view of the world. Paragraph 5.4.3 explains it was taken short because longer rates are "relatively high but forecast to steadily fall". MUFG's forecast in the next section has 5-year PWLB coming off from 4.80% in September 2025 to 4.30–4.40% through 2026-27 and 4.20% in 2027-28. The point at which the short call pays or costs is when that loan matures in April 2028 and has to be replaced. Sector-wide monthly drawdown activity — average rates, maturities, and how the shorter end has behaved since your report closed — is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity if it's ever useful context for where your £20m sat against everyone else's activity in the same window.

One thing we cannot tell you. Paragraph 5.4.2 flagged 22 December 2025 as a possible call date on the £5.255m LOBO. That date has passed, but this paper closes at 30 September and we do not hold a separate LOBO-call log for Argyll and Bute, so we can't state the outcome either way — only that the question is now answered somewhere in your records.

On the balance sheet the identity closes. Your revised paragraph 5.3.7 gives CFR £396m, Borrowing £187m and Other Long-term Liabilities £102m, and prints "Under Borrowing 107". Paragraph 5.3.8 confirms explicitly that this is the internal borrowing figure. The liability benchmark visualisation on our site handles that £107m — 27% of the £396m CFR — as a testable position rather than a settled one, which is the shape most useful when internal reserves are what defers external borrowing.

On training, two short courses fit what's above: PWLB explained, for anyone newer to the certainty-rate mechanics behind the £20m, and Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets, given your £5m fixed deposit to another authority puts you on the lending side of a market that some councils we've read use heavily. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, with free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find any of this useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Investment Strategy Mid-Year Review 2025-26, Argyll and Bute Council (Audit and Scrutiny Committee, 16 December 2025; Council, 29 January 2026).
